0.title: That You May Know: The Epistle of Assurance
0.overview:
There is a letter in the New Testament that reads like the heartbeat of an old man who has seen everything and lost nothing. John — the apostle whom Jesus loved, the one who leaned against the Lord at the Last Supper, the one who stood at the foot of the cross when the others had fled — writes at the end of a long life with the urgency of a man who knows that what he carries is the most important thing in the world. He has handled the Word of Life with his own hands. He has seen the glory. And he cannot be silent.

The First Epistle of John was written to a community under assault — not from Rome, but from within. Teachers had arisen who denied the full humanity of Christ, claiming that the eternal Son had not truly come in the flesh, that the spiritual and the material could not really meet. They were sophisticated, confident, and wrong. When they left the fellowship, John writes to those who remain, not to condemn the departed but to assure the faithful: you are not the ones who have missed it. The letter is saturated with the word "know" — used over thirty times. John wants his readers to know that they have eternal life, that they are in fellowship with the Father and the Son, that the darkness is passing and the true light is already shining.

But assurance in John is never cheap. It is tested by three great evidences that run through the letter like interwoven cords: the moral test (do you walk in the light, keeping his commandments?), the social test (do you love your brothers and sisters?), and the doctrinal test (do you confess that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh?). These are not conditions for salvation but symptoms of it — the fingerprints of new birth on a redeemed life. The person who has truly been born of God will love, will obey, and will confess. Not perfectly — John is the one who tells us that if we say we have no sin we deceive ourselves — but genuinely and persistently.

At the theological centre of the letter stands the cross. "The blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin" (1:7). "He is the propitiation for our sins" (2:2). "He laid down his life for us" (3:16). "God sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins" (4:10). John circles back to the atoning death of Christ again and again, because the cross is the ground of everything — fellowship, forgiveness, assurance, love. The love of God is not an abstraction in 1 John; it is a specific act: the sending of the Son into the world to bear the wrath that our sins deserved so that we might live through him.

The theological lens throughout this commentary is Reformed and christological, drawing especially on John Stott's The Letters of John (Tyndale New Testament Commentaries), D.A. Carson, Sinclair Ferguson, and the preaching of Alistair Begg. The governing conviction is that 1 John was written to produce settled, humble, joyful assurance in the hearts of those who have truly come to Christ — and that such assurance, far from producing complacency, is the very fire that fuels a life of love.

1.title: The Word of Life and the God of Light
1.text: <sup>1</sup>That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life — <sup>2</sup>the life was made manifest, and we have seen it, and testify to it and proclaim to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us — <sup>3</sup>that which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us; and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ. <sup>4</sup>And we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete. <sup>5</sup>This is the message we have heard from him and proclaim to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all. <sup>7</sup>But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin. <sup>8</sup>If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. <sup>9</sup>If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. <sup>10</sup>If we say we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.
1.overview:
The letter opens not with a greeting but with a declaration — the breathless, stacked-up proclamation of a man who cannot contain what he has witnessed. Four times John insists on the physicality of his testimony: heard, seen, looked upon, touched. This is no vision, no spiritual impression, no mystical encounter. The eternal Word who was with the Father before all worlds became touchable. John's hands rested on him. The Gnostic teachers who had just left the community claimed special spiritual knowledge that transcended the material. John's answer is the incarnation: the eternal life appeared, and we handled it with these hands.

From this foundation John moves to the purpose of his proclamation: fellowship — with the Father, with the Son, and with one another. And then, immediately, the first great test. The God with whom we claim fellowship is light — pure, uncompromising, all-revealing light. In him is no darkness at all. Any claim to fellowship with this God that allows a comfortable cohabitation with sin is self-deception. But the answer to sin is not despair — it is the blood of Jesus his Son, which cleanses continually (present tense) from all sin, and the promise of forgiveness to all who confess.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before John issues a single command or a single warning, he plants the whole epistle on the most astonishing fact in the history of the universe: God has made himself audible, visible, and tangible. The eternal Word — the one who was with the Father before the cosmos existed, the one in whom all things hold together — became the kind of thing that human hands could hold and human ears could hear. John is not theologising from a distance; he is writing as a man who was there, who sat beside him at meals, who saw the wounds after the resurrection, who touched what should not have been touchable. Every phrase in this prologue is a defiant, eyewitness insistence: this happened, in a body, in time, in our presence. And the breathtaking purpose of the proclamation is not merely that people would acquire correct information about God — it is that they would be drawn into the same fellowship that John himself shares with the Father and the Son. The God of infinite holiness has opened the circle of his own triune communion to creatures made of dust, and John’s joy — and God’s joy — is not complete until every reader enters in.
verseByVerse.theology: The Incarnation as the Ground of Fellowship. The physical language of the prologue — heard, seen, looked upon, touched — is not poetic decoration; it is the load-bearing structure of the gospel. John insists on the material reality of the Son’s coming because the redemption he brings is a redemption of the whole person, body and soul, in history and not merely in ideas. A Christ who never truly came in flesh cannot truly atone for flesh; a Christ who was not really seen cannot really be testified to; a Christ who was not really touched cannot really touch us. The incarnation is the event that makes fellowship with God possible — not a philosophical concept of divine-human union, but the specific, datable, locatable arrival of the eternal Son into the physical world he made.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: John writes into a crisis. Teachers were circulating in the churches of Asia Minor who were spiritualising Christ out of his humanity — the divine Christ, they said, descended on Jesus at baptism but departed before the crucifixion. The body was a vehicle, not a home. The stakes were everything: if he did not truly come in flesh, he did not truly suffer; if he did not truly suffer, there is no real atonement; if there is no real atonement, we are still in our sins. The prologue is a pastoral letter written to people whose salvation was being argued away.

Now: Every generation faces pressure to reshape Christ into something more palatable — more spiritual and less particular, more universal and less scandalously Jewish, more idea and less historical event. The intellectual instinct that wants a “Christ-principle” rather than the Son of Mary is not new. John’s answer has not changed: we proclaim what we heard, what we saw, what our hands handled. The gospel is not a philosophy; it is a report.

verseByVerse.quote: That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life—the life was made manifest, and we have seen it, and testify to it and proclaim to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us—
verseByVerse.commentary: The Greek sentence that opens the epistle is one long, breathless accumulation of sensory verbs before the main verb even arrives. John piles up the evidence: heard, seen, looked upon, touched. The variation is deliberate — heōrakamen (we have seen) is perfect tense, a completed action with ongoing significance; epsēlaphēsan (touched) is the most physical word possible, used of groping with the hands. The eternal Word was not a vision or a voice from heaven; he was handled. Verse 2 parenthetically identifies the subject: the life — the eternal life that was with the Father — was made manifest. The pre-existent Son entered time and became visible. John does not merely say he became knowable; he says he was seen, testified to, proclaimed. The testimony rests on sight, and the sight was real.

verseByVerse.quote: that which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us; and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: The main verb arrives at last: we proclaim. Everything John has heard and seen presses toward this act of proclamation, and the purpose of proclamation is not information transfer but relational inclusion: so that you too may have fellowship with us. The word koinōnia (fellowship, communion, sharing) describes not a social gathering but a participation in shared life. And John immediately unpacks what that fellowship is: it is fellowship with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ. The community of believers is not a human association that happens to worship God together; it is a community whose deepest reality is vertical communion with the persons of the Trinity. To enter the gospel is to be drawn into a circle of love that has been running from eternity.

verseByVerse.quote: And we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete.
verseByVerse.commentary: The stated purpose of the letter: joy. Not doctrinal correction for its own sake, not institutional self-preservation, not even the safety of the community — joy. And specifically our joy, which signals that the apostle’s joy is bound up with the reader’s flourishing. This is the pastoral heart beneath everything that follows: John writes because he cannot be fully glad until those he loves are fully in the fellowship of vv. 1–3. The complete joy echoes the High Priestly Prayer (“that my joy may be in them, and their joy may be full,” Jn 17:13), locating this joy not in favourable circumstances but in the shared life of the Son communicated to his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–10 — God Is Light: Walking in the Truth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first thing John says about God after the prologue is not a comfort — it is a blinding claim: God is light, and in him is no darkness at all. The double negation is absolute. There is no shadow in God, no moral ambiguity, no hidden corner of compromise. He is not mostly light, or light in the ways that count; he is light without remainder. This matters enormously because the rest of the passage consists of three statements that humans make in order to live comfortably without facing this light: we have fellowship with him while walking in darkness; we have no sin; we have not sinned. Each claim is named for what it is — a lie, a self-deception, a slander against God himself. But the passage is not an accusation without a remedy. The blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin (v. 7); the faithful and just God forgives and purifies those who confess (v. 9). The light that exposes is also the light that heals. God’s absolute holiness is not the barrier to fellowship; it is the very thing that makes genuine, unashamed fellowship possible, because he has provided in Christ everything the light reveals we need.
verseByVerse.theology: The Holiness of God and the Atonement. “God is light” is a doctrinal claim before it is an experiential one. It establishes the character of the God with whom fellowship is being offered: he is morally absolute, without shadow, without compromise. This means that fellowship with him is not a matter of lowered standards but of transformed persons. The atonement is therefore not God relaxing his demands; it is God, at infinite cost, providing the cleansing that his own character requires. The faithfulness and justice of v. 9 — the grounds for forgiveness — point directly to the cross: God is just to forgive because the penalty has already been borne. He does not forgive by overlooking sin; he forgives by having absorbed it in the death of his Son.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers John opposes claimed a spiritual illumination that placed them beyond ordinary moral accountability — their “knowledge” elevated them above the common categories of sin and confession. John’s three “if we say” tests directly expose this posture: to claim fellowship with God while living in moral darkness, to deny the existence of sin in oneself, or to deny a personal history of sin, is not spiritual advancement but spiritual self-destruction.

Now: The temptations of vv. 6, 8, and 10 are perennial. We insulate ourselves from the light by compartmentalising our lives (fellowship with God over here, the darkness of this habit over there). We deny present sinfulness by comparing ourselves to worse people. We deny a past of sin by reframing it as trauma, circumstance, or growth. John’s remedy is neither self-flagellation nor despair: it is the honesty of confession, met by the extravagant faithfulness of a God who has already paid for what we confess.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the message we have heard from him and proclaim to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.
verseByVerse.commentary: The governing premise of the entire epistle compressed into one sentence. God is light — not a god of light, not a god who uses light as a symbol, but one whose very being is characterised by the absolute moral purity, transparent truthfulness, and life-giving presence that “light” carries throughout Scripture (Ps 27:1; 36:9; Is 60:19–20). The emphatic double negation — darkness in him there is none at all — rules out any hidden zone of divine compromise. This claim did not originate with John; it is the message he heard from him — from Christ himself, who called himself the light of the world (Jn 8:12) and whose life made the claim visible. Everything the epistle teaches about sin, love, and fellowship is grounded here: in the absolute moral character of the God with whom we seek communion.

verseByVerse.quote: If we say we have fellowship with him while we walk in darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary: The first of three “if we say” tests (vv. 6, 8, 10), each naming a lie that protects the ego at the cost of reality. Walk (peripatōmen) is the habitual, directional movement of a life — not an occasional stumble but a sustained orientation. To claim intimacy with the God who is light while the pattern and direction of life runs toward darkness is not a theological error; it is a lie. The phrase “do not practice the truth” is striking: truth in John is not merely believed but done, lived out, embodied. A professed relationship with God that does not produce a truthful, light-oriented life is self-refuting. Calvin: “The test of our profession is always the habitual direction of the life, not the warmth of our feeling.”

verseByVerse.quote: But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.
verseByVerse.commentary: The positive counterpart to v. 6, and it contains two gifts that neither walking-in-darkness person can access: genuine fellowship with other believers, and ongoing cleansing by Christ’s blood. Walking in the light does not mean sinless perfection; it means living openly before God with nothing hidden, no zone of the life sealed off from his gaze. The standard is arresting: as he is in the light — God’s own transparency is the model. And even for those who walk in the light, the blood of Jesus is continuously needed: cleanses is present tense, continuous action. The blood of Christ is not a one-time transaction but a permanent provision, because even those living honestly before God remain sinners who need ongoing atonement.

verseByVerse.quote: If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
verseByVerse.commentary: The second false claim: not “I have never sinned” (past, v. 10) but “I have no sin” — present, ongoing, systemic sinfulness denied. The Gnostic opponents were likely claiming that spiritual illumination had elevated them beyond the category of sin. John’s answer is blunt: this is self-deception. The word planōmen (we lead ourselves astray) suggests active misdirection of the self — the deceit begins within. And its symptom is that “the truth is not in us”: the word of God, which plainly diagnoses every human being as a sinner (Ps 143:2; Rom 3:23), has not taken up residence in such a person. Claimed superiority to sin is actually evidence of the most basic spiritual failure.

verseByVerse.quote: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary: The most generous verse in the chapter. Over against self-deception (v. 8) John sets the promise of honest confession: God is faithful and just to forgive. Not merely willing — morally obligated by his own character and covenant. Faithful: he promised forgiveness through Christ and has staked his name on it. Just: because the penalty for sin has been fully paid at the cross, forgiving the confessor is not a waiving of justice but its satisfaction — the justice has already been executed on the Son. Stott: “It is not mercy but justice which God exercises in forgiving our sins, because the death of Christ has made it possible for him to be both just and the justifier.” The cleansing promised covers not merely specific sins confessed but all unrighteousness — the deeper contamination beneath the surface acts.

verseByVerse.quote: If we say we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.
verseByVerse.commentary: The third false claim, and the most extreme: not merely denying present sinfulness (v. 8) but denying any personal history of sin — “we have not sinned” in the past, ever, at all. To claim this is to contradict God’s own testimony about the human race (Rom 3:23; Ps 14:3), which is to call God a liar. John does not soften this: refusing the universal diagnosis of sin is not an honest difference of opinion but an accusation against the truthfulness of God. The consequence — “his word is not in us” — echoes v. 8 and ties back to v. 5. The person whose life leaves no room for the remedy of v. 9 has not yet received the message of v. 5. The good news has not yet reached them because the bad news has not yet landed.

1.theology:
The Incarnation as Foundation. Everything in 1 John rests on the physical, historical, tangible reality of the incarnation. John's stacked verbs in verses 1–2 — heard, seen, looked upon, touched — are a theological rampart against every form of docetism (the heresy that Christ only appeared to be human). If Christ did not truly come in flesh, the blood shed on Calvary has no atoning value, the resurrection is a spirit's trick, and there is no real fellowship between God and humanity. The incarnation is not incidental to Christianity; it is its structural foundation. God became graspable so that we could grasp him — and through him, life.

The God Who is Light. John's declaration that "God is light, and in him is no darkness at all" has massive ethical implications. Fellowship with a God of absolute moral purity cannot coexist with a comfortable relationship with sin. The light of God is not a comfortable mood but a searching, penetrating, all-revealing reality. It is also a liberating one: in the light, where our sin is exposed, the blood of Jesus cleanses. Reformed theology has always insisted on the holiness of God as the backdrop against which the grace of God becomes luminous. You cannot appreciate the gospel without first standing in the light of who God is.
1.examples:
Then: The community John writes to had just experienced a painful split. People they had worshipped with, broken bread with, called brothers and sisters, had walked out. The departure of the false teachers left wounds and questions. Were the ones who stayed the ones who had missed the deeper truth? John's answer in chapter 1 is the apostolic testimony: we were there. We heard him, saw him, touched him. This is not speculation; it is witness. The assurance of the community rests not on their spiritual experiences but on the testimony of those who were eyewitnesses of the Word of Life.

Now: We live in a culture that treats the interior life as the truest life — feelings, impressions, spiritual experiences. The incarnation is John's counter-word: Christianity is tethered to history, to flesh, to blood, to an empty tomb. Our fellowship with God is not a feeling; it is a fact grounded in the historical reality of the Son of God made flesh. And the practice of confession — agreeing with God about what we are — is the daily discipline that keeps that fellowship living and real. Every day we come back to the same place: not to earn forgiveness, but to receive what has already been purchased.

2.title: Our Advocate, Our Obedience, Our Love
2.text: <sup>1</sup>My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. <sup>2</sup>He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world. <sup>3</sup>And by this we know that we have come to know him, if we keep his commandments. <sup>5</sup>But whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God is perfected. By this we may know that we are in him: <sup>6</sup>whoever says he abides in him ought to walk in the same way in which he walked. <sup>15</sup>Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. <sup>16</sup>For all that is in the world — the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life — is not from the Father but is from the world. <sup>17</sup>And the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever. <sup>24</sup>Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, then you too will abide in the Son and in the Father. <sup>25</sup>And this is the promise that he made to us — eternal life.
2.overview:
Chapter 2 moves in three great movements. First, the pastoral heart of John: he wants his readers not to sin, but he is realistic enough to know they will, and he points them to the one who stands as their advocate before the Father — Jesus Christ the righteous, the propitiation for their sins. This is the most concentrated statement of substitutionary atonement in the Johannine letters, and it is placed here, at the beginning, as the ground of all that follows.

Second, John introduces the first of his three great tests of authentic Christianity: the test of obedience. Not sinless perfection, but a life characterized by the keeping of his commandments. The person who says "I know him" but does not keep his word is a liar. Third, John warns against the love of the world — a love that competes with and displaces the love of the Father. The world and all its desires are passing away; the one who does the will of God abides forever. The chapter ends with an appeal to hold fast to what was heard from the beginning: the apostolic gospel, not the novel teaching of the antichrists who have gone out.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Advocate and the Test of Knowing God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John opens chapter 2 with a pastoral masterpiece of balance. His aim is holiness — he writes so that his people will not sin. But he has been walking with Christ long enough to know that the command must arrive with a provision already in place: if anyone does sin, we have an advocate. The word is paraklētos — one called alongside, the same word Jesus used for the Holy Spirit (Jn 14:16), now applied to himself in his heavenly intercession. He stands before the Father, not pleading our innocence (we have none) but pleading his own righteousness. And he is not only advocate; he is propitiation — the atoning sacrifice that turns aside the wrath we deserved and makes the holy God’s embrace of sinners an act of justice, not compromise. The scope of this propitiation — not for ours only but for the sins of the whole world — is the widest possible invitation: no sinner is beyond the reach of what he has done. From this foundation of grace John then asks the first test: do you know him? Not know about him — know him. And the test, characteristically, is not a feeling but a pattern: whoever keeps his commandments and walks as he walked.
verseByVerse.theology: Propitiation: The Heart of the Atonement. Hilasmos (propitiation, v. 2) is the word John uses again in 4:10 and is among the most theologically precise words in the New Testament. It means not merely the covering of sin (expiation) but the turning aside of righteous wrath. God’s holiness demands that sin be dealt with; his love provides the means: the Son absorbs the penalty that holiness requires, so that the Father can righteously embrace the sinner. This is why forgiveness is not merely the setting aside of offences but an act of justice (1:9 — “faithful and just to forgive”). The cross satisfies the law and liberates the sinner simultaneously. Any account of the atonement that omits the turning aside of wrath is not yet the full gospel.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers in John’s world separated the divine Christ from the suffering Jesus, which meant the cross carried no real atoning weight. John’s insistence on propitiation — that this Jesus, the Christ, is the hilasmos — was a direct counter to that move. If the divine and human are separated in Christ, the atonement dissolves.

Now: Modern reticence about divine wrath often produces a gospel of divine sympathy without substitution — God understands us rather than saves us. John’s propitiation-language is the corrective: the good news is not that God has decided to overlook sin, but that he has borne its full penalty in the death of his Son. That is why it is news worth proclaiming.

verseByVerse.quote: My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary: The pastoral tone is set immediately: my little children (teknia mou) — the most intimate address in the epistle, a term of deep affection from the aged apostle to those in his spiritual care. The double purpose of the verse holds two truths in tension that must never be collapsed into each other. The first: John writes so they will not sin — holiness is the aim, and anything less is a lowering of the standard. The second: the provision for when they do sin is already in place. The advocate is not an emergency measure; he is the permanent, present reality of Jesus Christ the righteous, standing before the Father on behalf of the imperfect. The title “the righteous” is the ground of his advocacy: he pleads not our righteousness but his own.

verseByVerse.quote: He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world.
verseByVerse.commentary: The advocate of v. 1 is also the propitiation — the atoning sacrifice that satisfies the holy wrath of God against sin. He does not merely plead; he has already paid. The advocacy in heaven rests on the atonement accomplished on earth. And the scope breaks open every boundary: not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world. This is not a declaration of universal salvation but of universal sufficiency and universal offer: the atoning death of Christ is not a small, tribal provision that might run out — it is adequate for every human being who has ever lived, and the offer genuinely goes to all. No sinner stands outside the reach of what Christ has done; the only question is whether they come to him by faith.

verseByVerse.quote: And by this we know that we have come to know him, if we keep his commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary: The first explicit test of assurance: the evidence of genuine knowledge of God is obedience to his commandments. The Greek egnōkamen (we have come to know) is perfect tense — a knowledge acquired and still possessed, ongoing in the present. John is not setting up a works-based salvation; he is describing the organic consequence of genuine relationship. The one who truly knows God — in the relational, life-sharing sense John always means — will naturally, inevitably begin to keep his commandments, because the will is being aligned with the will of the one known. Keller: the test is not whether we ever fail (we do), but whether obedience is the settled direction of desire and effort.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever says ‘I know him’ but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him, but whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God is perfected. By this we may know that we are in him:
verseByVerse.commentary: The two sides of v. 3 sharpened into contrasts. The person who claims to know God while living in habitual disobedience is simply lying — the claim and the life are irreconcilable, and John has no interest in diplomatic softening. But the positive carries its own surprising beauty: where the word of God is kept, the love of God is “perfected” — brought to its intended completion, its telos. God’s love does not declare us righteous and then leave us as we were; it works inward until it reaches full expression in a life shaped by his word. And the final clause of v. 5, easily missed, is crucial: by this we may know that we are in him. Kept commands are not merely moral evidence; they are assurance of union. Obedience tells us we are in him, not just that we agree with him.

verseByVerse.quote: whoever says he abides in him ought to walk in the same way in which he walked.
verseByVerse.commentary: The claim to “abide in him” carries a precise ethical obligation: the concrete, historical pattern of Christ’s own walk becomes the measure. The aorist ekeinos periepatēsen (he walked) looks back to the specific life of the incarnate Son — not a mystical ideal but the observable, recorded pattern of his obedience, his love, his servanthood, his prayerfulness, his willingness to lose his life. The imitation of Christ is not self-improvement by willpower but the natural consequence of genuine union with him: those who truly abide in the vine begin to live like the vine. Where the walk diverges radically and permanently from his, the claim to abide deserves scrutiny.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–11 — The Old-New Commandment: Love and Light
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John introduces the love commandment with a deliberate paradox that turns out to be one of the richest insights in the letter: the commandment he is about to give is simultaneously old and new. Old, because it was there from the beginning of Israel’s covenant life — love God, love neighbour; the community already knew it. New, because something has happened in Christ that made the old commandment glow with a light it never had before. “Love one another as I have loved you” (Jn 13:34) — the incarnation and the cross gave the command a content and a power it could not have before Golgotha. And John frames this new commandment within the great eschatological drama: the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining. The new age has dawned in Christ; the old order of hatred and darkness is being displaced. To love is to live in the reality of that new world, to participate in the light that is already breaking. The test of whether one is in the light or the darkness is not a feeling or a doctrine but a relationship: do you love your brother?
verseByVerse.theology: Eschatological Ethics. John’s “the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining” (v. 8) is a window into his ethical method: he grounds commands in eschatological realities. We love one another not merely because we are told to but because the new age — the age of light, of the Spirit, of the resurrection life — has already broken in through Christ. To live in hatred is not just sinful; it is anachronistic, a choice to live in a world that is passing away. To live in love is to live in the world that is coming, the world that is, in Christ, already here. New Testament ethics are always shaped by this “already”: we are commanded to be what we already are in Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers who had left the community (v. 19) demonstrated their spiritual condition not only by their doctrine but by the schism their departure caused. Division is darkness made visible. Conversely, the community that remained and continued to love one another was living proof that the light was real and present.

Now: The hatred John describes in v. 11 — the darkness that blinds so completely that the hater does not know where he is going — is recognisable in the church wherever old wounds are nursed, grudges are maintained, and contempt for fellow believers is dressed up as principle. The test is not theological sophistication but the state of our relationships. Do we love the specific, difficult, disappointing people God has placed in our community?

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, I am writing you no new commandment, but an old commandment that you had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word that you have heard.
verseByVerse.commentary: John addresses his readers as beloved (agapētoi) — the term of choice when he is about to make a major point. The love commandment is old: it was there from the beginning, rooted in Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18, known and received from the first preaching of the gospel they heard. John’s point is important pastorally: he is not introducing innovation. The false teachers offered new knowledge, superior insight, advanced teaching. John keeps returning to the original — what you had from the beginning, the word you have heard. The antidote to spiritual novelty is not more sophistication but deeper rootedness in the apostolic foundation already received.

verseByVerse.quote: At the same time, it is a new commandment that I am writing to you, which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.
verseByVerse.commentary: Yet the commandment is also genuinely new — not chronologically but eschatologically. In Christ the love commandment was filled with new content: “love one another as I have loved you” (Jn 13:34) means the cross is now the measure and the pattern of love. It is “true in him” because Christ embodied it perfectly, and “true in you” because the Spirit is now producing it in believers. The eschatological frame is vital: the darkness is already passing away, the true light is already shining. The new age has broken in; the old order is being displaced. To love is not moral effort against the grain of reality but participation in the age that has already, in Christ, arrived.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever says he is in the light and hates his brother is still in darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary: The claim to spiritual light is tested by the most concrete, most uncomfortable measure: the treatment of a fellow believer. Hatred of a brother while claiming illumination is not inconsistency or hypocrisy in the ordinary sense — it is evidence that the claimed light has never arrived. The present participle misōn (hating) indicates not a passing offence but a settled, habitual disposition. John does not allow the vertical to be separated from the horizontal: any spirituality that cultivates communion with God while maintaining contempt for the visible people God has placed in our lives is a spirituality of self-deception.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever loves his brother abides in the light, and in him there is no cause for stumbling.
verseByVerse.commentary: The positive: love for the brother is the evidence of abiding in the light, and it carries an unexpected personal benefit. In him there is no skandalon — no stumbling block, no cause for tripping. The image suggests that love keeps the moral vision clear: the one who loves walks without the misstep that hatred produces. Darkness makes people stumble because they cannot see where they are going (v. 11); love, which belongs to the light, keeps the moral footing sure. Stott observes that love and light mutually reinforce each other — the one who truly sees God (lives in his light) will love what God loves, and that love itself keeps the spiritual sight from clouding.

verseByVerse.quote: But whoever hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary: The grammar is relentless: is in the darkness (present state), walks in the darkness (habitual movement), does not know where he is going (lost orientation), the darkness has blinded his eyes (completed action with permanent effect). Hatred does not merely obscure spiritual sight momentarily; it destroys the capacity for it. The hater cannot see because the darkness he has chosen has made him unable to see. This is John’s description of the spiritual blindness that makes the departure of the false teachers (v. 19) both explicable and tragic: those who walk in hatred of the brothers lose the ability to find their way back to the light.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–14 — Assurance for Every Stage of Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the middle of a letter full of tests and warnings, John pauses to do something purely pastoral: he reminds everyone where they stand before God does anything else. He addresses three groups — little children, fathers, young men — and then repeats the address in a kind of antiphon, as though wanting to make sure every person in the community hears their name called. The pattern of what he says to each group is revealing. To the children (in faith), the first word is not a command but a declaration: your sins are forgiven. That is the foundation beneath everything else. The fathers are those who have accumulated depth — they know him who is from the beginning, and long knowing has not made them casual about Christ but more rooted in him. The young men are those blazing with energy and fight: they have overcome the evil one, and the word of God abides in them — Scripture is not just their source of information but their sword and their strength. John writes not to instruct each group about something new but to confirm them in what they already have: forgiveness, depth, strength. Assurance is the gift John gives before he gives any further commands.
verseByVerse.theology: Assurance as Pastoral Foundation. Calvin noted that exhortation addressed to the unforgiven produces only despair. John follows the same instinct: before he calls his people to anything, he reminds them of who they already are — forgiven, knowing, strong. Biblical assurance is not presumption; it is the appropriate response to the reliability of God’s promises and the reality of the new birth. The tests of the epistle (vv. 3, 5, 10, 14, etc.) are not hurdles to clear before assurance is granted; they are the visible evidence that the life of God is already present, confirming what God has already declared.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A community under pressure from false teachers needed to know that their standing before God did not depend on accepting the teachers’ claims. John’s affirmation of forgiveness, knowledge, and victory was a counter to the false teachers’ implicit message: that ordinary believers needed something more to be truly secure.

Now: Churches today can subtly communicate that assurance is only for the spiritually mature or the doctrinally sophisticated. John’s address to the “little children” is the corrective: the very first thing the newest believer needs to hear is not a command but a declaration. Your sins are forgiven for his name’s sake. Everything else builds on that.

verseByVerse.quote: I am writing to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven for his name’s sake.
verseByVerse.commentary: John addresses the whole community as teknia (little children) — his most affectionate term, used for all believers regardless of spiritual age. And the first thing he says to them is not a command or a warning but a declaration of grace: your sins are forgiven. The perfect tense (aphēontai) indicates a past act with ongoing effect — forgiven, and remaining forgiven. The ground is not their merit or their tenure in faith but his name’s sake — the person, character, and atoning work of Jesus Christ, whose name is the sole basis of every pardon. Forgiveness is the first word to every believer because it is the ground of every other word.

verseByVerse.quote: I am writing to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. I write to you, children, because you know the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary: Three addresses, three characterisations. The fathers are defined by depth of knowledge: you know him who is from the beginning — the eternal Christ, the one John introduced in the prologue. Long years in the faith have not produced familiarity that breeds contempt; they have produced rootedness in the person of Christ. The young men are defined by victory: you have overcome the evil one. The aorist speaks of a decisive triumph already won — not a battle still raging without result, but a real overcoming, in Christ. The children (here paidia, a different word suggesting those newer in faith) know the Father — the most basic Christian knowledge, the Abba-relationship granted in adoption.

verseByVerse.quote: I write to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary: John repeats the three-fold address (“I write” in the aorist, past tense, as opposed to the present tense of v. 13) — a liturgical intensification, as though the blessing must be said twice to be fully received. The fathers are confirmed in their knowledge of the eternal Christ; no new formula is added. The young men receive an expanded description: they are strong, the word of God abides in them, and they have overcome. The order is illuminating: strength is not the cause of Scripture-abiding but its result. The word of God dwelling in the young man is what makes him strong for the fight against the evil one. Scripture is not information about spiritual warfare; it is the weapon itself (Eph 6:17).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–17 — Do Not Love the World
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The command comes with a sharpness that must not be blunted: do not love the world. John is not calling for cultural withdrawal, intellectual narrowness, or ascetic rejection of created goods. He is identifying a specific enemy of the soul — the age organised in rebellion against God, with its own system of values, its own hierarchy of desires, its own account of what a good life looks like. And he is naming the three roots of this world-system with clinical precision: the desire of the flesh (appetite as ruler), the desire of the eyes (covetousness as creed), and the pride of life (self-sufficiency as religion). These are not peripheral temptations; they are the deep grammar of the fallen heart. Against this world, John sets the eschatological reality: it is passing away. The world is not merely morally wrong; it is temporally doomed. The whole age organised against God is being dissolved, already, from the inside, by the arrival of the one who overcame it. To love the world is to invest in a structure that is already collapsing. To do the will of God is to abide forever — to participate in the only permanence there is.
verseByVerse.theology: The World, the Flesh, and Temporality. John’s three-fold anatomy of worldliness in v. 16 — desires of the flesh, desires of the eyes, pride of life — maps onto Augustine’s account of concupiscence: the disordering of human desires away from God toward lesser goods. The created order is good; the appetite, the eyes, and the desire for status are not evil in themselves. What sin has done is redirect these capacities inward and downward, away from the Creator who is their proper end. The world-system takes these redirected capacities and builds a whole culture around them. The gospel does not destroy appetite and desire; it redirects them back to their proper object: God himself, in whom all genuine goods are found.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ephesus was a commercial hub and a temple city — the wealth and the religion of the world were both visibly on display. The desires of the flesh, the eyes, and the pride of life were not abstract temptations but daily architectural realities. John’s readers were not being asked to imagine worldliness; they were surrounded by it.

Now: The three roots John identifies are as active now as they were then, but the delivery mechanisms are more sophisticated — the endless scroll, the comparison economy of social media, the cult of self-expression and personal brand. The diagnosis of v. 16 has not aged. The remedy has not changed either: the person who does the will of God, whose desires have been reordered around the living God, is not destroyed by the world’s passing but freed by it.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.
verseByVerse.commentary: “The world” (kosmos) in this context is not the created order that God made and loves (Jn 3:16) but the age organised in rebellion against him — the system of values, allegiances, and desires that runs counter to the kingdom. The command is absolute: do not love it. And the reason is binary: love of the world and love of the Father are mutually exclusive. They cannot coexist in the same heart because they are pulling in opposite directions. Where the world-system holds the heart’s primary allegiance, the Father has no room. This is not a call to cultural hatred but to a radical re-ordering of ultimate loyalty: everything in the world may be received and enjoyed as God’s gift, but nothing in it may be enthroned as the heart’s supreme good.

verseByVerse.quote: For all that is in the world—the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life—is not from the Father but is from the world.
verseByVerse.commentary: John anatomises the world-system into three streams. The desires of the flesh: appetite as sovereign, the body’s cravings treated as moral authorities. The desires of the eyes: covetousness, the restless wanting of what is seen, the soul shaped by comparison and acquisition. Pride of life (alazونeia): the boasting arrogance of self-sufficiency — the person who needs no God because they have their own resources. None of these is from the Father: they are the distortions that sin introduced into capacities that were originally oriented toward God. Commentators from Augustine onward note the parallel with Genesis 3:6 — the fruit was “good for food” (flesh), “pleasing to the eyes” (eyes), “desirable to make one wise” (pride) — and with the temptation of Christ in Matthew 4. The world-system is very old, and so is its remedy.

verseByVerse.quote: And the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever.
verseByVerse.commentary: The decisive eschatological argument: the world is passing away — present tense, the process is already underway, already in motion. To love the world is to invest in a structure that is in the process of collapse. The contrast is stark: the one who does God’s will abides forever. The word menei (abides) is John’s characteristic term for the deepest relationship with God (2:6, 10, 27, 28; 4:13, 15, 16) — and here it is applied to the permanence of the person so related. The universe is ageing; the believer who does God’s will is being renewed. Sproul: “The universe is growing old; the believer who does God’s will is growing young.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — Antichrists, Apostasy, and the Anointing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John does something remarkable in this section: he turns a crisis of apostasy — people leaving the community, denying Christ, sowing confusion — into an occasion for confidence. Yes, antichrists have appeared; yes, the teachers who left were denying the Father and the Son; yes, there are those trying to deceive. But none of this catches God by surprise. The departure of the apostates was not a tragedy that nearly undid the plan — it was a revelation that made the true from the false plain. And more: the ordinary believers who remain have something the elite false teachers claimed to offer and could not deliver. They have the anointing of the Holy One. They all — every one of them, not just the theologically sophisticated — have the Spirit’s inner illumination. The Spirit who is truth teaches them what is true and keeps them in it. The answer to false teaching is not merely better argument; it is the Spirit of truth abiding in the community of those who know the Son and confess him. Abide in him — the repeated exhortation of vv. 24, 27, 28 — is at once a command, a promise, and the deepest protection available against every form of spiritual deception.
verseByVerse.theology: The Spirit’s Anointing and the Sufficiency of the Apostolic Word. John’s claim that believers “have no need that anyone should teach them” (v. 27) does not abolish the office of teacher in the church (cf. Eph 4:11). It means something more specific: they have no need of the supplementary, superior teaching the false prophets are offering. The Spirit’s anointing does not bring new revelation beyond the apostolic word; it illumines and confirms the word already received. This is the Reformed understanding of the testimonium Spiritus Sancti internum — the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit by which believers recognise and hold the truth of Scripture. The Spirit and the Word work together; neither operates independently.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers’ authority rested on their claimed superiority of knowledge (gnōsis). They implied that ordinary believers needed their guidance to reach the real truth. John’s “you all have knowledge” (v. 20) and “you have no need that anyone should teach you” (v. 27) were direct pastoral corrections: the Spirit given at conversion is adequate; the apostolic word already received is complete.

Now: The same dynamic appears wherever a teacher or movement implies that the ordinary Christian life — Scripture read, Spirit indwelt, community worshipping — is insufficient, and that some additional experience, technique, or revelation is needed for the real thing. John’s answer is the same: you have the anointing; it abides in you; the truth you received from the beginning is enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Children, it is the last hour, and as you have heard that antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have come. From this we know that it is the last hour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John names the theological moment: the last hour. Not a prediction but a declaration — the final era has arrived with the coming of Christ, and the appearance of antichrists confirms it. The repeated “it is the last hour” (opening and closing the verse) is rhetorical insistence: the time for comfortable neutrality has run out. The anticipated singular antichrist has been preceded by many antichrists in the community — not pagan outsiders but former insiders, making their theological deviation all the more urgent. John’s use of the plural is important: the spirit of antichrist is not a single future figure only but a recurring spiritual reality throughout the church age, present now in the community’s own midst.

The word antichristos is John’s own coinage — it appears nowhere before his letters and is found only in his correspondence in the entire New Testament (1 Jn 2:18, 22; 4:3; 2 Jn 7). The prefix anti carries two senses: ‘against’ (opponent) and ‘in place of’ (counterfeit substitute) — the antichrist is both an adversary of Christ and a false usurper who presents himself as an alternative Christ. Preachers should be ready to address the widespread assumption that John’s antichrists are identical to the ‘beast’ of Revelation 13, the ‘man of lawlessness’ of 2 Thessalonians 2, or the fourth beast of Daniel 7. These are different texts, using different Greek and Aramaic terms (to thērion, ‘the beast’; ho anthrōpos tēs anomias, ‘the man of lawlessness’), and possibly referring to different historical configurations. John himself never uses any of these terms. His antichristos is a theological category — the spirit of opposition to and substitution of the true Christ — which has manifested throughout the church age and will culminate in a final expression. The plural ‘antichrists’ already active in John’s own community confirms that his concern is not limited to a single end-times figure but embraces the recurring Christological denial that attacks the gospel in every generation.

verseByVerse.quote: They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us. But they went out, that it might become plain that they all are not of us.
verseByVerse.commentary: John’s interpretation of the departure is penetrating and pastorally honest. The apostates left; John does not pretend this was not painful or destabilising. But he interprets it: their leaving was not caused by external pressure or superior argument — it revealed an internal reality. They were never truly of the community, and the departure made this plain. The providence declared in “that it might become plain” is striking: even apostasy serves the purpose of God in separating what appeared united. Genuine belonging produces genuine perseverance; those who fall away finally demonstrate that they lacked the life they appeared to have. This is not comfortable, but it is clarifying.

verseByVerse.quote: But you have been anointed by the Holy One, and you all have knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary: The contrast is emphatic: but you. Set against the departed antichrists is the anointed community. The chrisma (anointing) from the Holy One — almost certainly the gift of the Holy Spirit given at conversion — is what gives believers the knowledge that the false teachers could only claim to offer. And John specifies the scope: you all have knowledge, not merely the teachers or the theologically trained. The Spirit’s illuminating work is the possession of every member of the body. The elitism of the false teachers — superior knowledge for the spiritually advanced — is quietly devastated: the ordinary believer, anointed by the Spirit, already has what the elite cannot provide.

verseByVerse.quote: I write to you, not because you do not know the truth, but because you know it, and because no lie is of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary: John clarifies the purpose of the letter: he writes not to inform the ignorant but to confirm what the readers already know. This is important for how the epistle functions — it is a letter of assurance and confirmation, not a course in basic Christianity. The readers already know the truth; what they need is to be reminded of it firmly enough to resist the deception circulating among them. The axiom “no lie is of the truth” is a logical claim with theological force: truth and falsehood are not on a spectrum. The false teaching is not a partial truth or a different angle on the same reality; it is simply incompatible with the truth. The readers’ knowledge of the truth equips them to recognise the lie by its incompatibility.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is the liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, he who denies the Father and the Son.
verseByVerse.commentary: John names the specific lie that identifies the antichrist: the denial that Jesus is the Christ. This is a Christological claim — not the denial of the existence of God but the severing of the human Jesus from the divine Christ. The likely background is a proto-Gnostic teaching that the divine Christ descended on Jesus at baptism but departed before the cross, leaving only a human to die. John’s answer is total: you cannot deny the Son and retain the Father. The two are inseparable in the economy of salvation. There is no access to the Father except through the Son (Jn 14:6); to reject the Son is to sever the only connection to the Father. The christological confession is not optional theology; it is the load-bearing wall of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: No one who denies the Son has the Father. Whoever confesses the Son has the Father also.
verseByVerse.commentary: The positive and negative stated with equal clarity and equal force. The Father and the Son are inseparable in the economy of salvation: access to one is access to the other; rejection of one is rejection of the other. This is not theological symmetry for its own sake but a statement about the structure of reality. The Son is not a pointer to the Father or a useful mediating concept that can be adjusted while the Father-relationship is kept intact; he is the only way the Father is known, loved, and reached. Confessing the Son is therefore the indispensable act of all true religion — not a supplementary option for those who prefer a more Christocentric spirituality, but the very hinge on which everything else turns.

verseByVerse.quote: Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, then you too will abide in the Son and in the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary: The antidote to false teaching, restated: tenacious retention of the original apostolic word. “From the beginning” is John’s refrain throughout ch. 2 — it is both a temporal marker (the gospel received at conversion) and a polemical point (against the false teachers who offer the new). The conditional is structured as a promise: if the original message abides, then you will abide — in the Son and in the Father. Holding fast to right doctrine is not merely intellectual hygiene; it is the means of holding fast to the persons of the Trinity. The word and the relationship cannot be separated: abide in the truth, and you abide in the one who is truth.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the promise that he made to us—eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary: The content of the apostolic message reduced to its essential promise: eternal life. Not eternal existence (which the unbeliever also has in a tragic sense) but the life of the age to come — God’s own life shared with his people, already begun in those who believe (Jn 5:24, “has passed from death to life”). This promise is secured not by the believer’s faithfulness in holding it but by the faithfulness of the one who made it. And the connection to vv. 23–24 is explicit: the eternal life is in the Son (5:11–12), so abiding in the Son is the way of possessing the promise. What the false teachers offer is a detour away from the one in whom the promise resides.

verseByVerse.quote: I write these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you.
verseByVerse.commentary: John states his pastoral purpose plainly: the false teachers are not merely mistaken — they are trying to deceive. The word planōntōn (those leading astray) uses the same root as “we deceive ourselves” (1:8): self-deception and active deception are the two faces of the same spiritual disorder. John does not soften this. Naming the threat clearly is an act of pastoral love; it equips the community to resist rather than absorb the false teaching out of misplaced charity. The most dangerous deceptions in the church are usually the ones that are not identified as deceptions, because they arrive wrapped in spiritual language and appealing sincerity.

verseByVerse.quote: But the anointing that you received from him abides in you, and you have no need that anyone should teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about everything, and is true, and is no lie—just as it has taught you, abide in him.
verseByVerse.commentary: John does not mean the community needs no teachers at all (Eph 4:11 is still in the canon); he means they have no need of the supplementary elite knowledge being offered by the false teachers. The Spirit’s anointing — the internal illumination given to every believer at conversion — teaches about everything that pertains to salvation and godliness. Not new revelation, but the Spirit-enabled recognition and appropriation of the apostolic word already received. The verse ends as the chapter will end: abide in him. The remedy for every form of false teaching is not intellectual victory but sustained union with the Son, kept by the Spirit, anchored in the word received from the beginning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–29 — Abide in Him: The Returning King and the Family Likeness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter closes with the horizon it has been approaching all along: the return of Christ. Everything John has said about abiding, about keeping commandments, about loving the brother, about resisting false teachers — all of it is now framed by the appearing of the one in whom the believer abides. At that appearing there will be either parrēsia (bold, unashamed confidence) or shrinking in shame. Which it will be is determined not in that moment but in the habitual posture of the life between now and then. And the final verse opens the door into chapter 3 with a theological principle that will carry the weight of the next major section: if God is righteous, then those born of him will practice righteousness. The new birth is not merely a change of status; it is a change of nature, and that nature tends toward the character of the one who gave it. Family resemblance is theological, not merely moral: we live like God’s children because we are God’s children.
verseByVerse.theology: Eschatological Motivation for Present Obedience. John’s appeal to the Parousia (v. 28) is a characteristic New Testament move: the return of Christ is not a distant abstraction but the event that gives weight and direction to all present choices. The New Testament writers consistently motivate holiness by the coming of Christ, not merely by moral duty. The appearing of Christ is the moment when the hiddenness of the believer’s life in God will be made visible (Col 3:4); the one who has abided in him will have nothing to hide and every reason for confidence. This is not works-righteousness; the confidence is not earned by moral performance but by genuine union with Christ maintained through faith.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers had effectively short-circuited eschatological seriousness by claiming that their superior knowledge had already brought believers into the fullness of what was coming. John’s reminder that Christ is still to appear — and that his appearing will reveal all — restores the appropriate weight to present faithfulness.

Now: When the return of Christ recedes from the church’s active consciousness, the motivation for sustained, costly obedience weakens. John’s final word to ch. 2 is a re-ignition of that consciousness: he is coming. Abide in him now, so that when he appears you may have confidence and not shrink from him in shame.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, little children, abide in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not shrink from him in shame at his coming.
verseByVerse.commentary: The exhortation to abide has accumulated force through the chapter (vv. 6, 10, 24, 27) and now reaches its eschatological grounding. When he appears — the Parousia, the return of Christ, is the event toward which the whole Christian life is oriented. At that appearing there will be parrēsia — bold, open-faced confidence before the one who is coming — or there will be the shrinking of shame. John includes himself in both possibilities (“we may have confidence... not shrink”), refusing to exempt the apostle from the same eschatological seriousness. The confidence is not earned by perfection but by genuine, persistent abiding in Christ; the shame is not punishment from without but the inevitable awkwardness of meeting the one whose commands you spent your life ignoring.

verseByVerse.quote: If you know that he is righteous, you may be sure that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him.
verseByVerse.commentary: A key theological hinge connecting ch. 2 to ch. 3. The logic is Christological: God is righteous; therefore, those born of him will practice righteousness. The new birth is not merely a change of legal status (though it is that) but a change of nature — the divine life implanted in the believer tends inevitably toward the character of the one who gave it. Family resemblance is the evidence of genuine birth. The verse does not say that practicing righteousness earns the new birth; it says that genuine birth from the righteous God produces the practice of righteousness. This is John’s first mention of the new birth in the epistle, and it sets the stage for the extended treatment in 3:4–10.

2.theology:
Advocacy and Propitiation. The paired terms of 2:1–2 give us the two aspects of Christ's saving work seen from different angles. As advocate, he represents us before the Father — our case is in his hands, and he is qualified to plead it because he is righteous. As propitiation, he has already dealt with the ground of the accusation — the wrath of God against our sin has been absorbed at the cross. These are not two separate acts but two perspectives on the one act of the cross. The same sacrifice that satisfied divine justice now grounds our ongoing access to divine mercy. Reformed theology has always insisted that the atonement is both objective (propitiation — something accomplished outside us, in history, on a cross) and applied (advocacy — an ongoing ministry of Christ on our behalf). Both are necessary; together they produce the settled assurance John wants his readers to have.

The Three Tests. John's three tests — obedience (2:3–6), love (2:9–11), and belief (2:22–23) — are not a checklist for earning assurance but symptoms of new birth. Just as a doctor looks for signs of life, John looks for the signs that genuine regeneration has occurred. These tests are not meant to produce anxiety but clarity: not "have I been good enough?" but "is there genuine fruit of the Spirit in my life?" The tests are cumulative and mutually reinforcing — genuine obedience produces love; genuine love flows from right belief; genuine belief manifests in how we treat the brothers and sisters.
2.examples:
Then: The antichrists who had left the community had claimed a superior knowledge of God. Their departure seemed, to some, like the enlightened ones leaving the unenlightened behind. John's response is pastoral and pointed: the ones who left proved by their leaving that they were never truly of the community (2:19). This is not cruelty but theology — genuine new birth produces perseverance. The ones who remained, confused and perhaps diminished, were the ones who had "the anointing from the Holy One" and knew the truth (2:20). The test of authenticity is not sophistication but faithfulness to the beginning.

Now: We live in a world of novelty — new spiritualities, new therapies, new paths to self-actualization. The church is perpetually tempted to trade the apostolic gospel for something more culturally current, more psychologically satisfying, more intellectually respectable. John's word is the same: let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. The gospel does not need to be updated; it needs to be inhabited. The depth we seek is not found by moving beyond the cross — it is found by going deeper into it.

3.title: Children of God, Love in Deed
3.text: <sup>1</sup>See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are. The reason why the world does not know us is that it did not know him. <sup>2</sup>Beloved, we are God's children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. <sup>3</sup>And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure. <sup>14</sup>We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. <sup>16</sup>By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers. <sup>17</sup>But if anyone has the world's goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God's love abide in him? <sup>18</sup>Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth.
3.overview:
Chapter 3 opens with one of the most arresting exclamations in all of Scripture: See what kind of love — the Greek word suggests something foreign, exotic, surprising, from another world entirely. The love that makes sinful creatures children of the holy God is not an extension of ordinary human affection. It is a different category of love altogether, an invasion from another realm. And it is not merely a legal status: "we are" — present tense, already, actually, really. The children of God are hidden to the world because the world did not recognize the Son of God either. The family resemblance is not yet complete — what we will be has not appeared — but the hope of Christlikeness at the appearing shapes the life of the believer now.

The chapter then descends from the heights of adoption to the concrete test of love: do we lay down our lives for the brothers? John defines love not by a feeling but by the cross — "he laid down his life for us" — and then applies the definition with bracing directness: if you have material resources and see a brother in need and close your heart, how does the love of God abide in you? Love in deed and truth, not in word and talk. The cross makes love costly, and costly love is the mark of those who have truly understood the cross.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Children of God: Now and Not Yet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The opening word of this chapter is a command to look: See — behold, consider carefully, let this land. What we are to see is the kind of love the Father has given. The Greek word potapēn (what kind of) is used of things foreign, extraordinary, belonging to a different category altogether — the sort of thing that makes you say, “Where does this come from? This is not from here.” And what is this extraordinary love? That we should be called children of God. Called — yes. But John will not let it rest there: and so we are. Not called in courtesy or in aspiration; actually, really, ontologically children of the living God. The declaration is followed immediately by its consequence: the world does not know us, because it did not know him. The family resemblance to a Father the world has rejected makes his children strange to the world, and this is not a problem to be solved but a reality to be understood. Then the chapter lifts its eyes to the horizon: we are children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared — but we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. The beatific vision is not the reward for becoming like Christ; it is the very event that accomplishes the final transformation. And the hope of that appearing is not passive; it is purifying: everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure. The eschatological future is already pressing back into the present, shaping us now into the image of the one we will see then.
verseByVerse.theology: Adoption and the Beatific Vision. The children-of-God language in v. 1 is not a metaphor for a warm relationship; it is a legal and ontological declaration. Adoption in the Roman world conferred full inheritance rights and a genuine change of family identity. The believer is not God’s friend or God’s admirer; the believer is God’s child. The future dimension (v. 2) takes this to its completion: we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. The Reformed tradition has always held that this final transformation into Christ’s likeness is simultaneous with the direct vision of God — not a prerequisite for it. We will not first become holy enough to see him; seeing him will make us holy. The visio Dei is not the prize at the end of sanctification; it is the event that completes it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers in John’s world were offering a kind of spiritual completion in the present — a knowledge that brought the fullness of the divine life now, without remainder. John’s “what we will be has not yet appeared” is a deliberate correction: no one in this age has yet received the fullness. The “already” is real (we are children now), but the “not yet” is equally real. Any teaching that collapses the not-yet into the already is a distortion of the gospel.

Now: The purifying hope of v. 3 is one of the most practical verses in the letter. The person who genuinely expects to see Christ — who lives in the light of that appearing — is being shaped toward his likeness now, in daily choices, in the direction of desire, in what they are becoming. Eschatology is the most powerful ethical force in the New Testament: we become what we behold, and we behold what we love. Love the appearing of Christ, and the appearing will already be beginning to do its work in you.

verseByVerse.quote: See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are. The reason why the world does not know us is that it did not know him.
verseByVerse.commentary: Idete — see, look, consider carefully: an imperative demanding active attention. The wonder John is pointing to is not a doctrine to be filed away but a reality to be marvelled at. Potapēn (what kind of) is used in the New Testament of things foreign and extraordinary — the disciples used it of the waves obeying Christ (Mk 4:41). This love does not come from the world; it comes from outside it. Its content: we are called children of God — and John adds the two most important words in the verse: and so we are. The calling is not a courtesy title but a declaration of reality. The world’s failure to recognise us follows necessarily: having rejected the Father, it cannot recognise his children. The family resemblance to a rejected Father makes his children strangers in the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, we are God's children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.
verseByVerse.commentary: The now-and-not-yet of Christian existence held in perfect tension. We are God’s children now — present tense, certain, already in effect. But what we will be has not yet appeared — the full expression of that sonship lies beyond the veil of this age. The revealing event is the appearing of Christ: when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. The direction of causality is crucial: the vision of Christ produces the likeness, not the other way around. The glorified Christ, seen face to face without the mediation of faith and without the distortion of our present fallen perception, will accomplish in an instant what a lifetime of sanctification has been working toward. Sproul: “We will not first become worthy to behold him; beholding him will make us worthy.”

verseByVerse.quote: And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure.
verseByVerse.commentary: Eschatological hope is not passive. The one who genuinely hopes for the appearing of Christ — who lives in the light of v. 2 — purifies himself now, in the present, in the daily direction of life. The hope pulls the future into the present and makes it morally formative. The standard is arresting: as he is pure — not “as pure as humanly possible” but with Christ’s own purity as the target. This is not perfectionism in the sense of achieved sinlessness (1:8 has ruled that out definitively) but perfectionism in the sense of orientation: the genuine hope of seeing Christ trains the moral eye on his character as the goal toward which the life is being shaped. Where the hope of his appearing is alive, moral seriousness is alive.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–10 — Sin, the Devil, and the New Birth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This section is the theological heart of 1 John’s teaching on sin and the new birth, and it must be read carefully or it will either terrify the genuine believer or comfort the false one. John is making a cosmic claim: there are two families in the world, and they are distinguished by what they do. Behind every life of sin stands the devil — not as an excuse, but as an explanation of origin. The devil has been sinning from the beginning; those whose lives are oriented toward sin bear his family pattern. But then comes the great declaration that should make every believer shout: the reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil. He came into the devil’s domain, entered the world the devil thought he owned, took on flesh the devil thought he had corrupted, and from inside the ruin began the demolition. Every work the devil has built — sin, death, bondage, accusation — is under destruction. And the new birth is the mechanism by which that destruction reaches individual human lives: God’s seed abides in the one born of him, a living principle of divine life that is fundamentally incompatible with the pattern of sin. John is not teaching sinless perfection; he is teaching that the direction and orientation of the regenerate life is away from sin and toward God, because the life of God is now within. The children of God and the children of the devil are known by their practice — what they do with their sins, their righteousness, and their brothers.
verseByVerse.theology: The New Birth as Ontological Change. John’s “God’s seed abides in him” (v. 9) is one of the most striking metaphors in the epistle.
