Eternal life is not a commodity distributed independently of Christ; it is a person-located reality. This is why “having the Son” (v. 12) and “having life” are the same thing: to be in Christ is to have the life; to be outside Christ is to be outside the life. No formula, no ritual, no spiritual discipline, no religious achievement can transfer the life apart from the Son in whom it resides.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.
verseByVerse.commentary: The starkest binary in the epistle and one of the sharpest in the New Testament. Not “more or less life” depending on spiritual development; not “life of different quality” depending on doctrinal precision — has or does not have, life or not life. The Son is either possessed (by faith, in union) or he is not, and life follows the Son without remainder. This is both the most inclusive possible invitation (anyone, from any background, may have the Son by faith) and the most exclusive possible statement (no other means of possessing life exists). To soften this binary is not pastoral generosity but a failure of love: it leaves people comfortable in a condition John has just described as the absence of life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — Knowing What We Have in Christ: Assurance, Prayer, and the True God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John states the purpose of the epistle in v. 13 with a simplicity that should stop us in our tracks: I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life. Not hope, not suspect, not feel on good days — know. The whole letter has been building toward this confidence, providing the tests by which the genuine believer may be assured of what they have. And now the assured believer is shown what they may do with their assurance: pray with boldness (vv. 14–15), intercede for sinning brothers (vv. 16–17), and live in the certainty of three great “we know” truths that the letter has been establishing. We know that the one born of God does not keep on sinning — the new birth is real and its effects are real. We know that we are from God, and the whole world lies in the evil one — we live in hostile territory, but we are not of it. And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true — the great circle closes. The letter that opened with eyewitness testimony to the eternal Word made touchable ends with the declaration that this Word has come, has given us minds and hearts to know the true God, and is himself the true God and eternal life. The last command — little children, keep yourselves from idols — is not an afterthought; it is the practical corollary of everything that has come before. You have the true God. Do not settle for anything less.
verseByVerse.theology: Assurance as the Fruit of the Gospel, Not Its Presumption. The assurance John offers in v. 13 is grounded not in human confidence or moral achievement but in the reliability of the one who gave the promise. The tests of the epistle — keeping the commandments, loving the brothers, confessing the Son — are not hurdles to clear before assurance is granted; they are the visible evidence of the invisible new birth that God has declared. Assurance is not the same as certainty of personal infallibility (1:8–10 has ruled that out); it is the confidence that the God who began the work will complete it (Phil 1:6), that the one who gave the Son will freely give all things (Rom 8:32), that the life given in the Son cannot be taken away by anything in all creation (Rom 8:38–39).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers had implicitly undermined the assurance of ordinary believers by suggesting that their ordinary faith was insufficient. John’s final summary of what we know is a direct pastoral restoration: you know you have eternal life; you know the Son of God has come; you know you are from God. The confident epistemic language (“we know”, vv. 18, 19, 20) is the language of assurance grounded in apostolic testimony and Spirit-confirmation, not in claimed superiority.

Now: The final verse — “little children, keep yourselves from idols” — sounds abrupt after the theological heights of v. 20. But it is exactly right. The best safeguard against idols is a clear, deep, Christ-centred knowledge of the true God. The person who has genuinely encountered “him who is true” and understood that “he is the true God and eternal life” has been given the greatest possible protection against every substitute. You cannot treasure what is real and be satisfied with counterfeits — but you must know what is real. This is the final purpose of the epistle: that you know him, and knowing him, refuse every idol.

verseByVerse.quote: I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary: The stated purpose of the entire letter. John writes not to evangelise but to assure — his audience already believes, and what they need is confidence in what believing gives them. That you may know — not hope, not feel, not reasonably expect — know (eidēte, with the certainty of direct perception). The knowledge John offers is not the hidden mystical knowledge of the opponents; it is the plain, testable, Spirit-confirmed knowledge that comes from believing in the name of the Son of God and living the life the epistle has described. Assurance is not presumption; it is the appropriate response to the reliability of God’s word about his Son.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us.
verseByVerse.commentary: The assured believer of v. 13 immediately has a posture toward God in prayer: parrēsia — bold, open, unashamed confidence. The condition of answered prayer — according to his will — is not a limiting clause designed to lower expectations but a clarifying one: prayer aligned with God’s will is prayer that will certainly be heard. The shift this produces is from “will God hear me?” (anxious petitioning) to “what is God’s will?” (collaborative alignment). The person who knows God through his word and Spirit can pray with confidence not because they have mastered a formula but because they are asking in the direction God is already moving.

verseByVerse.quote: And if we know that he hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests that we have asked of him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The logic of v. 14 pressed to its conclusion: if God hears (v. 14), the requests are granted. The present tense “we have the requests” is striking — not “we will have” but “we have,” even before the visible answer appears. This is the confidence of faith that takes God at his word: the one who has asked according to his will can live in the certainty of the answer because God’s hearing is itself the act of granting. This is not a blank cheque for any desire labelled “prayer”; it is the confident posture of the person whose asking has been shaped by the God they know.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he shall ask, and God will give him life—to those who commit sins that do not lead to death. There is sin that leads to death; I do not say that one should pray for that. All wrongdoing is sin, but there is sin that does not lead to death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The most exegetically contested passage in the letter. The confident intercession of vv. 14–15 is immediately applied to the most painful of pastoral situations: a sinning brother. John commands intercession for the brother committing sin “not leading to death” — most likely the ordinary failures and sins of genuine believers, for which repentance and forgiveness remain available (1:9). “Sin leading to death” is most likely the settled, unrepentant denial of Christ by those who have definitively left the community (2:19; 4:2–3) — the final, hardened apostasy. John does not forbid prayer for such persons but does not command it, recognising a possible point of no return. The positive pastoral point stands: when you see a struggling brother, intercede. God gives life through the prayers of the community.

The ‘sin leading to death’ (hamartia pros thanaton) is one of the most contested phrases in the letter, and a preacher must be prepared to address three main interpretive streams. First, a patristic tradition, drawing on Matthew 12:31–32, identifies it with the unpardonable sin — the settled, conscious rejection of the Spirit’s testimony to Christ, the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. Second, some interpreters read thanatos as physical death: God has, in extreme cases, executed believers through direct divine judgment for persistent, serious sin (1 Cor 11:30; Acts 5:1–11; 1 Cor 5:5); on this reading the warning concerns divine discipline, not spiritual damnation. Third, the Reformed majority view reads it as hardened, final apostasy — the definitive departure from Christ described in 2:19 and 4:3, by those who have so thoroughly repudiated the Son that they are beyond the reach of restoration. John’s ‘I do not say that one should pray for that’ is not a prohibition of intercession but a pastoral honesty: the prayer for restoration presupposes that the person still stands where restoration is possible. John declines to prescribe a prayer that implies a return is in process when the evidence suggests no such openness exists — while also declining to forbid it. The positive pastoral point of vv. 16–17 is therefore not exhausted by the difficult exception: when you see a struggling, sinning brother, intercede; God gives life through the prayers of his people.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that everyone who has been born of God does not keep on sinning, but he who was born of God protects him, and the evil one does not touch him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The first of three climactic “we know” statements. The born-of-God believer does not keep on sinning — the habitual orientation of the regenerate life is away from sin, not settled into it (cf. 3:9). The protection is personal: “he who was born of God keeps him” — almost certainly a reference to Christ the Son, the one who was uniquely born of God, who guards his own (Jn 10:28–29; 17:12). The evil one does not touch (haptetai) him — does not lay hold of, does not gain a controlling grip. This is not a promise of immunity from temptation or spiritual attack, but of ultimate invulnerability: the evil one cannot finally own or destroy the one Christ is keeping. The believer is not unassailed; they are undefeatable.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that we are from God, and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary: The second “we know”: the epistle’s binary in its sharpest possible form. We are from God; the whole world lies in the evil one. The word keitai (lies) suggests passive submission — the world is not actively fighting the evil one but resting in his embrace, unaware and unresisting, like a sleeping person in the arms of an enemy. There is no neutral ground, no comfortable middle category, no third territory between the two domains. The believer lives in a world under hostile power, sustained only by the greater one within them (4:4), witnessing to a world that does not yet know it needs rescuing from the one it is resting in.

verseByVerse.quote: And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true; and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary: The third and culminating “we know”: the Son of God has come. The incarnation — the great fact with which the epistle opened (1:1–2) — is restated as the ground of everything. He has come, and the coming has given us understanding (dianoian) — not merely information but the cognitive and spiritual capacity to know the true God. The circle from the prologue is now complete: the eternal life that was with the Father and was made manifest (1:2) is now declared to be the true God himself. The ascription of deity to Jesus Christ — “He is the true God and eternal life” — is among the clearest in the New Testament. The one in whom we are, the one who is eternal life (v. 11), the one the Father sent — he is the true God. No qualification, no reservation.

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, keep yourselves from idols.
verseByVerse.commentary: The most abrupt closing in the New Testament — and exactly right. After the theological summit of v. 20 — the true God, eternal life, the Son who has come — John ends with the most practical of warnings: guard yourselves from idols. An idol is anything that claims the place that belongs to the true God — any competing love, any false conception of God, any teacher who offers a Christ less than the one described in v. 20. In Ephesus, literal idols were everywhere; the command was not metaphorical. But the principle applies in every age and every culture: having encountered the true God, refuse every substitute. The best protection against idols is not vigilance alone but the deep, sustained, Spirit-confirmed knowledge of the one who is true. You cannot treasure the real and be satisfied with the counterfeit. Little children, keep yourselves from idols.

5.theology:
Faith as Victory. The declaration of 5:4 — "this is the victory that has overcome the world — our faith" — is one of the most important statements about the nature of faith in Scripture. Faith is not a spiritual achievement, a heightened state of consciousness, or a moral virtue we cultivate. It is a hand that receives, a trust that rests, a confidence that looks away from itself to the Son of God who has already overcome. The perfect tense — "has overcome" — points to the finished work of Christ at the cross as the source and ground of the believer's victory. We do not overcome the world by spiritual heroism; we overcome it by trusting the one who already has.

Assurance as Gift. The stated purpose of the letter — "that you may know that you have eternal life" (5:13) — stands as a rebuke to every theology that treats Christian assurance as presumption or spiritual pride. John writes to produce certainty. Reformed theology has always distinguished between assurance and presumption: presumption claims safety without evidence; assurance rests on the testimony of the Spirit, the evidence of new birth, and the promises of God. The three tests of the letter are not meant to produce anxiety but confirmation — the gentle hand of a faithful pastor showing the believer where the signs of life are visible. To know that you have eternal life is not arrogance; it is the appropriate response to the faithfulness of the God who cannot lie.
5.examples:
Then: The community, battered by false teaching and painful departure, needed to know one thing above all: that they had not missed it, that they were in the Son, that the life they had received was real and was eternal. John writes to give them that certainty — not a new experience, not a higher spirituality, but the settled confidence of those who have the Son and therefore have life. The simplicity of the final verdict — "whoever has the Son has life" — is both the most inclusive and most exclusive statement possible: inclusive, because anyone may have the Son; exclusive, because there is no life outside of him.

Now: In an age of therapeutic Christianity, where the goal is often feeling good about ourselves, John's letter is a corrective and a comfort. Assurance in John is not a feeling to be cultivated; it is a knowledge to be received — grounded in the testimony of God himself (5:9–10), confirmed by the evidence of new birth, and resting ultimately on the person of the Son. "This is the true God and eternal life" — Jesus Christ, the same yesterday, today, and forever. Whatever else may be uncertain in a Christian life, this is not: whoever has the Son has life, and the Son cannot be taken away.
